chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Madani, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the prayer in Ramadan in the mosques. He said: "When the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) arrived in Kufa, he ordered al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) to announce to the people: 'There is no congregational prayer in the mosques during the month of Ramadan.' So al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) announced to the people what his Commander had ordered. When the people heard al-Hasan ibn Ali's statement, they cried out, 'O Umarah! O Umarah!' When al-Hasan returned to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), he said to him, 'What is this noise?' He said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, the people are crying out, O Umarah! O Umarah!' The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said, 'Tell them to pray.'"

Thus, when the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) disapproved, he disapproved of the congregation (collective gathering) and did not disapprove of the prayer itself. When he saw that the matter was becoming corrupted for him and the people were being tested (fitnah), he permitted it and ordered them to pray according to their custom. All of this is clear, praise be to God.

key_terms.يَا عُمَرَاهْ: O Umarah (an exclamation referring to Umar ibn al-Khattab, indicating imitation of his practice)

ai.seo_question: What was the reason for the temporary prohibition of congregational prayers in Ramadan during the time of Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the principle of *al-sabr ala al-mashiqah* (enduring minor displeasure to prevent greater harm) in Shia jurisprudence, where Imam Ali (AS) temporarily suspended the congregational Tarawih to avoid sectarian friction with the Umayyad loyalists in Kufa. The people's exclamation 'O Umarah' highlights their perception of Ali’s action as a deviation from the established Sunnah of Umar ibn al-Khattab, demonstrating the political sensitivity of ritual practices in early Islamic history. Ultimately, Ali’s reversal confirms that the prohibition was contextual (*muqayyad*) rather than absolute, affirming the validity of congregational Ramadan prayers when communal harmony is preserved.
